newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jet again fires at Iraqi missile site.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jet again fires at Iraqi missile site.

text.p: A U.S. F-16 fighter fired a missile at an Iraqi anti-aircraft site on Monday when the pilot received indications his plane was being targeted in the second such incident in three days, the Pentagon said.
Iraq denied that either incident had occurred. It accused the White House of a ploy to boost President Bill Clinton's re-election bid on Tuesday.

The Defence Department had said on Sunday that the first U.S. attack, which occurred on Saturday in the same no-fly zone in southern Iraq, was a mistake because an investigation indicated Iraqi gunners had not targeted the F-16.

Defence Secretary William Perry warned Iraq on Monday that U.S. jets would defend themselves, but the White House and Perry said there was no indication Iraq was playing a cat-and-mouse game with allied jets patrolling no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq.

"(Iraq's President) Saddam Hussein has very clear warning already from the fact that we conduct 100 sorties (flights) a day over this area" of southern Iraq, Perry told reporters in response to questions at the Pentagon.
"We conduct them with airplanes that are very well armed and quite capable of taking care of themselves," he said.
The United States has warned Iraq not to threaten U.S. and other allied pilots patrolling the zones, established after the Gulf War to restrict Iraqi military activity.

"They (pilots) will continue with the rules of engagement that they now have," said Perry. "If their warning equipment on the airplane indicates that they are being tracked, they are authorised to launch anti-radiation missiles at the site."
He said it was not known yet whether the U.S. "Harm" high-speed anti-radiation missiles had struck Iraqi batteries and that both incidents were under investigation.
Navy Commander Joe March, a Defence Department spokesman, said Monday's missile firing took place at about noon Iraq time (0900 GMT) about 25 miles (40 km) from where Saturday's incident occured.

Perry said both incidents occurred south of the 32nd parallel and that the southern zone had been very quiet for at least a week before the shooting, with no indication Iraq was increasing activity against U.S. and allied jets.
"We don't see any pattern here that the situation has changed," said White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry on Monday on a Clinton campaign visit to Manchester, New Hampshire.

Iraq's official news agency INA, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation and quoting a Foreign Ministry source, on Monday denied the Pentagon report that the second jet had fired a missile. Over the weekend it also denied the first incident, saying the story was to boost Clinton at the polls.

The Pentagon issued a statement late on Sunday saying that "further analysis of Saturday's incident involving a U.S. aircraft over southern Iraq has not substantiated initial indications of Iraqi radar activity."
A Pentagon spokesman said it was unclear whether the radar activity picked up by instruments aboard the Air Force F-16 was due to an equipment malfunction.
But he defended the pilot's actions, saying he "acted appropriately" in accordance with rules of engagement.

The United States expanded the southern zone northward from the 32nd to the 33rd parallel, up to the outskirts of Baghdad, in September after a confrontation with Washington because Saddam sent troops into northern Iraq to back one Kurdish faction against another.
Washington also responded to the incursion by attacking southern Iraq with 44 ship- and air-launched cruise missiles.
